name: Anomalous origin of a coronary artery
aliases: anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery

reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / ESC Guidelines on Adult Congenital Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: A congenital anomaly in which a coronary artery arises from the wrong aortic sinus or the opposite coronary artery, with a wide spectrum of clinical significance
The high-risk variant is an interarterial course, where the anomalous vessel passes between the aorta and pulmonary artery and may be compressed during exertion
It is an important cause of exertional chest pain, syncope, arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death in young athletes, sometimes as the first presentation
An anomalous left coronary arising from the right sinus with an interarterial course is generally regarded as higher risk than the corresponding right-sided anomaly
Many cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons
CT coronary angiography best delineates the ostial anatomy, the course relative to the great vessels, and high-risk features such as a slit-like ostium or intramural segment
Surgical repair (for example unroofing or reimplantation) is considered for high-risk anatomy or symptoms attributable to the anomaly
reference.pathophysiology: Anomalous origin of a coronary artery is a defect of coronary embryological development in which a coronary ostium arises from an inappropriate aortic sinus or from the opposite coronary. The clinical danger of certain variants arises from the anomalous vessel taking an interarterial course between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. During exertion the aortic root expands and the increased flow demands widen these great vessels, which can compress the interarterial segment; an associated acute-angle take-off, slit-like ostium, or intramural course within the aortic wall further compromises the lumen. The resulting dynamic reduction in coronary flow can precipitate myocardial ischaemia, malignant arrhythmia, and sudden death, characteristically during or just after strenuous activity, which is why exertional symptoms in a young person warrant careful evaluation.
additionalInvestigations: CT coronary angiography to define ostial origin, interarterial course, and high-risk morphology
Cardiac MRI for anatomy and assessment of ischaemia or scar
Stress testing or stress imaging to seek inducible ischaemia
Invasive coronary angiography where anatomy remains unclear
Echocardiography to assess ventricular function and exclude other structural disease
Ambulatory ECG monitoring for exertional arrhythmia
redFlags: Exertional syncope or presyncope in a young person
Exertional chest pain or documented ischaemia attributable to the anomaly
Aborted sudden cardiac death or malignant ventricular arrhythmia
High-risk anatomy such as an interarterial or intramural course with a slit-like ostium
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely with the specific anatomy; many variants are benign and require no intervention, whereas a high-risk interarterial course carries a real risk of sudden cardiac death, particularly during vigorous exertion. Appropriately selected surgical repair can relieve symptoms and reduce risk, and activity guidance is an important part of management.
pitfalls: Attributing exertional syncope in a young athlete to a benign cause and missing the anomaly
Failing to characterise the course relative to the great vessels and the presence of an intramural segment
Assuming a normal resting ECG or stress test excludes a dangerous anomaly
Overtreating clearly benign variants with unnecessary surgery
Neglecting individualised exercise restriction advice pending evaluation
references: ESC Guidelines for the Management of Adult Congenital Heart Disease
management: Risk-stratify by anatomy using CT coronary angiography to identify high-risk features such as an interarterial course, intramural segment or slit-like ostium
Offer surgical repair, such as unroofing, reimplantation or bypass grafting, for high-risk symptomatic interarterial anatomy
Advise restriction from competitive and strenuous exertion in high-risk unrepaired patients given the risk of exertional sudden cardiac death
Manage benign low-risk variants conservatively with observation and reassurance
Evaluate for inducible ischaemia with stress imaging and treat anginal symptoms with anti-ischaemic agents such as beta-blockers where appropriate
Refer to a cardiology or congenital heart disease multidisciplinary team and counsel on sudden death risk
Maintain surveillance and escalate for new exertional chest pain, syncope or arrhythmia
